turns:
=== CALL C0021 ===
Abdul: Hello, hello! Can you hear me okay?
Nilesh: Yeah, I can hear you fine. Hi.
Abdul: Good, good. I'm Abdul. How are you doing today?
Nilesh: Not bad, thanks. Bit knackered, to be honest. I was on a late last night, so, erm, yeah. You?
Abdul: Late shift? Yeah, me also, yesterday! I'm a porter at the hospital in Whitechapel, and the lifts in the old block broke down again, so I'm pushing the beds round the long way, you know, half the building. My legs are telling me about it today.
Nilesh: Oh no. That sounds rough.
Abdul: It's okay, it's the job, innit. Sixteen years I'm doing it. What about you, what you do?
Nilesh: Erm, I work in a factory, chilled food, in Park Royal. I run a tray-sealing machine on the packing line. Ready meals, that sort of thing.
Abdul: Ah, so the ones in the supermarket, the little trays with the film on top?
Nilesh: Yeah, that's us. Well, some of them. I've been there eleven years now, so I sort of... I train the new starters on the sealer as well, when they come in.
Abdul: Eleven years, that's good, that's loyal. Same as me, they give me the new porters to show around, because I know every corridor. You must be patient, yeah? To train people.
Nilesh: I try to be. Erm, when I started someone was a bit sharp with me, and I remember how that felt, so I just take it slow with them, you know. Nobody learns anything if they're scared of the machine.
Abdul: Exactly, exactly. Same with patients. Old lady, she's frightened going down to the scan, I just keep talking, talking, about the weather, cricket, anything. By the time we get there she's forgot she was worried.
Nilesh: That's nice, actually. I reckon the nurses must like you.
Abdul: They ask for me by name sometimes! Makes me feel very important. Do you follow cricket at all?
Nilesh: Yeah, more than football really. I listen to the Tests on the radio app on my break. Though England... another collapse, wasn't it.
Abdul: Don't talk to me about collapse! Bangladesh, last week, I was sure, sure they're going to win. I told my friends, I said relax, this one is easy. Then three wickets in two overs. Finished.
Nilesh: Oh, I saw that. That was painful.
Abdul: Painful, yes. I used to play, Sunday tape-ball in Victoria Park, but my knees, after forty-five, they said no more, Abdul. Now I just umpire. Shout at everybody instead.
Nilesh: Ha. I play five-a-side with my cousins every couple of weeks, but they stick me in goal, so I don't have to run much.
Abdul: Smart man! Goalkeeper is the best job. And the puzzle at the start, how did you find it? I was stuck on the third one a long time.
Nilesh: Erm, the one with the shapes? Yeah, I didn't finish it, to be honest. I sort of guessed the last two.
Abdul: Me too, guessing! I put my glasses on, I thought they would help, but no.
Nilesh: Ha, yeah. Do you get many days off, with the rota?
Abdul: Not so many. I am saving my leave, I go back to Sylhet every two, three years, so I take one month together. You have family round you?
Nilesh: Yeah, my parents are in Kenton, ten minutes away. My mum keeps sending food round, which, erm, I'm not complaining about. My dad's... he's slowing down a bit lately, so it's good being close, you know.
Abdul: That's a blessing, being close. Really. Look after him. You only get them once.
Nilesh: Yeah. I try.
Abdul: You're a good son, I can tell. So do you cover shifts, at your place, when they ask?
Nilesh: Erm, more than I should, probably. I find it hard to say no, sort of, and then I'm—

=== CALL C0022 ===
Marta: Hi! Hello, can you hear me? Sorry, I think I was on mute for a second.
Gurpreet: Yes, yes, I can hear you. Hello. How are you?
Marta: I'm good, thank you, a bit shattered, but good. I'm Marta. And you're Gurpreet?
Gurpreet: Yeah, Gurpreet. Nice to meet you. You had busy day?
Marta: Erm, sort of, yeah. I'm a pharmacist at a hospital, on the cardiology wards, so it's lots of checking drug charts and talking to patients before they go home, you know, explaining their blood thinners and things. And the Victoria line this morning was absolutely rammed, I had someone's elbow in my face the whole way. What about you, what do you do?
Gurpreet: Er, I work in factory near Heathrow. Food packaging. I run the tray-sealing line, for ready meals, sandwiches, like that.
Marta: Oh, so the sandwiches people buy at the airport?
Gurpreet: Yeah, yeah, some of them going to airport, some supermarket. I'm part-time now, three shifts in a week.
Marta: That sounds quite nice, actually, part-time. Is that your choice?
Gurpreet: Er, yeah, sort of. I hurt my back two years ago, so the physio said little bit less. It's okay now. Little bit hard sometimes, but okay.
Marta: Oh, I'm sorry. Backs are horrible, honestly. We see so many people on the ward who've been, you know, lifting things for thirty years. Do you do exercises for it?
Gurpreet: I walk. Lake Farm, near my place, in Hayes. I do slow lap, every day off. That's it, really.
Marta: That's lovely. I swim, or I try to, twice a week before work, but the pool in Leyton is always freezing, so sometimes I kind of stand at the edge and think about it and then go home.
Gurpreet: Ha. Cold water, no, I can't.
Marta: And what do you do on the weekends, apart from walking?
Gurpreet: Sunday I go gurdwara in Southall, mostly. And I'm growing chillies and coriander in pots, on the patio. This year chillies are doing really well, I don't know why.
Marta: No way! I'm growing tomatoes in our tiny garden and they've finally, finally gone red. I was so excited I sent a photo to my mum in Poland.
Gurpreet: Ah, you're from Poland? Nice.
Marta: Yeah, from Gdańsk, but I've been here fifteen years now, so I'm kind of half and half. What chillies are they?
Gurpreet: Er, green ones, the small hot ones, like we use in India. My partner Simran says too many now, we have to give to neighbours.
Marta: That's the best problem to have. Is Simran into the gardening too?
Gurpreet: Not so much. She's teaching assistant, primary school, so she's tired after work, the kids, you know. She likes eating the chillies, not growing.
Marta: Ha, yeah, no, totally. My husband's the same with my tomatoes, he just appears when they're ready. He's a teacher as well, actually, geography. He spends the whole weekend marking at the kitchen table, and our cat sits on the paper.
Gurpreet: You have cat?
Marta: We do, Pierogi. He's a tabby and he's, erm, a bit round. He knocks everything off the worktop, one thing a day, like it's his job.
Gurpreet: Pierogi, like the food?
Marta: Exactly like the food! Polish dumplings. He looks like one, honestly. Sorry, I'm talking so much. How did you find the puzzle at the start?
Gurpreet: Er, it was okay. Last one was hard, I took long time. I think maybe I got it.
Marta: Better than me, I gave up on the last one and just stared at it.
Gurpreet: That's okay, no problem. Everybody is like that, innit, with puzzles. Like my cousin, he—

=== CALL C0023 ===
Hitesh: Hello! Yeah, there he is. Can you hear me, uncle? Sorry, sorry, can I call you uncle? Your photo, you look like proper uncle.
Abdul: Ha! Yes, yes, call me what you like. Abdul. Everybody at work calls me uncle anyway, even the doctors.
Hitesh: Hitesh. Peterborough. Where you are?
Abdul: Leyton, East London. Thirty years I'm in East London. You're in Peterborough, very nice. What you do there?
Hitesh: Factory, chilled food, I'm on flow-wrap machine. Basically I'm the guy who knows how to fix it when it jams, you know, supervisor comes to me. Part-time, but that's my choice, yeah, because I do delivery also, and my own business ideas, so.
Abdul: Business ideas! Good, good. What kind of business?
Hitesh: Er, phones, maybe. I used to work in my cousin's phone shop back home, Gujarat, I can unlock anything, fix screen, anything. Or taxi licence. Or, you know, investments.
Abdul: Investments, ah. Shares and all that?
Hitesh: Bit of crypto, bit of shares. Some up, some down, that's the game, innit. You have to be in it.
Abdul: Me, I don't understand it. My money goes in the bank and then to my sister's kids for school. That's my investment.
Hitesh: That's also good, mate. Safe. What's your job?
Abdul: Hospital porter, Whitechapel. Sixteen years. Pushing beds, wheelchairs, oxygen, everything. Twenty thousand steps a shift, my shoes finished every few months.
Hitesh: Twenty thousand! You don't need gym then.
Abdul: No gym. The hospital is my gym. You play any sport?
Hitesh: Cricket, mate. Sunday, tape-ball, in the park, with the guys. Mostly for the banter, but I'm good, I bowl fast. And IPL, every match. Mumbai Indians.
Abdul: Mumbai! Ah. I play tape-ball also, Victoria Park, until my knees said no. Now I umpire. And I'm Bangladesh, of course.
Hitesh: Bangladesh, oh no. Sorry, uncle. Last week, that match...
Abdul: Don't. I was talking about this one already today with the gentleman before, Nilesh. Three wickets in two overs. I am still not sleeping properly.
Hitesh: Ha! At least they lost properly. Mumbai, last night, our guy drops simple catch. Simple! My son Dev could catch that, and he's twelve. I was shouting at the TV, my wife says the neighbours will complain.
Abdul: The umpire in me says it's a hard catch maybe. The fan in me says, no, he should catch.
Hitesh: No, no, uncle, no hard catch. Straight in the hands. I was saying to my brother on WhatsApp, this guy should be dropped himself. Big argument in the family group now.
Abdul: Family group, yes, we have one too, everybody in Sylhet, everybody in London, all shouting. You have big family here?
Hitesh: Brother in Leicester. He has shop there. Doing well, you know, he's... yeah, he's doing well. Parents are in India still. My father, er, his health is not so great now.
Abdul: Ah. I'm sorry to hear. You go back often?
Hitesh: Every two, three years, for the weddings mostly. Should be more. But tickets, holidays, work, you know how it is.
Abdul: I know. I know exactly. Me also, I save one month leave, then go. It's never enough. Call him a lot, that's what I say. Phone is free now.
Hitesh: Yeah. Yeah, I do. My wife says I talk more to the cricket than to my dad, but... anyway. Sorry, sorry, what was the question? I'm going everywhere.
Abdul: No question! We are just chatting, it's fine. Tell me, the puzzle at the start, you finished it?
Hitesh: Puzzle, honestly, mate, waste of time. I did the first two fast, then the last one, I thought, who is checking? I just clicked something.
Abdul: Ha! Same as Nilesh, he's guessing also. I think nobody finished, only the researchers.
Hitesh: They make it, so they know the answer, innit. Easy for them. Like my supervisor, he makes the rules, then he—

=== CALL C0024 ===
Nilesh: Hi. Hello. Can you hear me alright?
Gurpreet: Yes, I can hear you. Hello. How are you?
Nilesh: Yeah, not bad, thanks. Bit tired. You?
Gurpreet: I'm okay, thank you. Little bit tired also. I'm Gurpreet.
Nilesh: Nilesh. Nice to meet you.
Gurpreet: Nice to meet you. Where you are, which area?
Nilesh: Kingsbury, North West London. You?
Gurpreet: Hayes. West side, near Heathrow.
Nilesh: Oh right, not too far then. What do you do?
Gurpreet: I work in food factory, packaging, near the airport. I run the tray-sealing line.
Nilesh: No way. Tray-sealing? That's what I do. Park Royal, chilled food. Ready meals mostly.
Gurpreet: Really? Same machine! Ready meals, sandwiches, yeah, yeah.
Nilesh: That's funny. The man I spoke to before, Abdul, he asked me about the little trays with the film on top, and I was trying to explain, and now here's someone who actually knows.
Gurpreet: Ha. Nobody knows what we do, really. They just buy the lasagne.
Nilesh: Exactly. Erm, how long have you been doing it?
Gurpreet: Er, long time, maybe ten years, different places. Now I'm part-time, three shifts, because my back. I hurt it two years ago, so the physio said, you know, little bit less.
Nilesh: Oh, sorry to hear that. Was it at work?
Gurpreet: Yeah, sort of. Lifting the film rolls, I think, too many times wrong way. It's okay now. Little bit hard sometimes.
Nilesh: Yeah, those rolls are heavy. We had a lad do the same last year. I always tell the new starters, get the trolley, don't be a hero, you know.
Gurpreet: Yeah, yeah, good advice. You train the new people?
Nilesh: Yeah, on the sealer, mostly. They keep asking me. I don't mind, really. They're thinking about team leader for me, maybe, but erm, I'm not sure. Half the line are my mates, so telling them off would be, sort of, weird.
Gurpreet: I did team leader cover one time. Two weeks. Very hard. One guy always late, I have to talk to him, I don't like it. I'm happy to go back to machine.
Nilesh: Yeah, that's exactly what worries me. The money would be nice, though. We're trying to save for a deposit, so.
Gurpreet: Same, me and Simran, my partner. We are saving. London is very expensive, so maybe Slough, something small.
Nilesh: Yeah. It feels like it's always just out of reach, you know.
Gurpreet: Yeah. Slowly, slowly. That's it, really.
Nilesh: Do they change your overtime rota a lot? Ours changes every week.
Gurpreet: Every week! I look on Monday, it's one thing, Wednesday, something else. And people ask me to swap, I always say yes.
Nilesh: Ha, me too. I can't say no. My wife says I should, but then I'm stood there and they look at you, and—

=== CALL C0025 ===
Hitesh: Hello! Yes, I can see you. The happy lady with the books!
Marta: Ha! That's me, yeah. Hi, I'm Marta. Sorry, the books are a bit of a mess, I keep meaning to sort them out.
Hitesh: No, no, it looks good. My daughter Riya, she's eight, she wants a shelf like that. Hitesh, Peterborough. Where you're from? I hear little bit accent.
Marta: Yeah, Poland, Gdańsk, but I've lived in London fifteen years now. Walthamstow. What about you?
Hitesh: Gujarat, India. Came 2008, I married, wife's family was in Peterborough, so, Peterborough. What's your job?
Marta: I'm a pharmacist, in a hospital, on the heart wards. Erm, so I check everyone's medication and talk to patients before they go home.
Hitesh: Pharmacist! My wife, Komal, she works in pharmacy also. Counter, in the shop. She knows all the tablets, she tells me what to take, I don't listen.
Marta: Ha, that's what all my patients say about their wives. Does she enjoy it?
Hitesh: Yeah, she likes it. Full-time. She's the organised one, you know, bills, school forms, holidays, everything. Me, I'm the fun one.
Marta: Every house needs both, honestly. I'm the organised one in ours. I plan our holidays on spreadsheets, my husband just turns up at the airport.
Hitesh: Spreadsheet for holiday! No, mate. Too much. You just go.
Marta: I know, I know, but I like it, it's kind of half the fun for me. Where do you like to go?
Hitesh: India, mostly, weddings. Blackpool with the kids, London. And Dubai, my friend works there, I'm going this year. Definitely. Well, I say every year.
Marta: Oh, you should, though. Who books it, you or Komal?
Hitesh: Komal, obviously. Then I complain about flight time. Six in the morning, why, who flies six in the morning?
Marta: People who get the cheap flights! Sorry, that sounded like a spreadsheet person.
Hitesh: Ha! Yes, very spreadsheet. What you do, then, I'm in factory, flow-wrap machine, part-time. I do delivery also, moped, evenings. Good money, you know, if you know the right areas.
Marta: Oh, so you're working quite a lot of hours then, with both?
Hitesh: Er, depends. Part-time is my choice. Rules at the factory, mate, half of them pointless. Supervisor wants you standing there even when the machine is running perfectly.
Marta: I mean, we have loads of rules on the ward too, and some of them do feel a bit silly, but, erm, usually there's a story behind each one. Someone got hurt once, you know.
Hitesh: Maybe. Maybe. But some of them, no story, just somebody in an office. Anyway. Did you do the puzzle?
Marta: Badly. I gave up on the last one. Gurpreet, who I spoke to first, was much more patient than me.
Hitesh: Gurpreet, he looks like he knows his stuff. I just clicked anything. Uncle Abdul, he also, guessing. Nobody finished, I think.
Marta: That makes me feel better, honestly. So what do you do to relax, when you're not working?
Hitesh: Cricket. Watching, playing, Sunday in the park. And last night, Mumbai Indians, our guy drops simple catch, I'm still angry.
Marta: I don't really know cricket, to be honest, but my husband's English, so I've been made to watch some. It goes on for days, right?
Hitesh: Test, yes, five days, that's for old men. IPL is three hours, fast, everybody hitting sixes. Much better. You watch one with me, I explain, you'll love it.
Marta: Okay, deal, but you have to sit through a whole Polish volleyball match with—

=== CALL C0026 ===
Abdul: Hello, hello! Gurpreet, yes?
Gurpreet: Yes, hello. How are you?
Abdul: Good, good, thank you. Abdul, from Leyton. And how are you, my friend?
Gurpreet: I'm okay, thank you. I saw your photo, you have chillies on balcony, yeah?
Abdul: Yes! You saw them! Nobody notices my chillies. Yes, few pots. This year better than last year.
Gurpreet: Me also. I grow chillies and coriander, on the patio, Hayes. This year very good, too many. Simran says give to neighbours.
Abdul: Same, same! What kind you grow?
Gurpreet: Green ones, small, the hot ones. From India seeds, my cousin brought.
Abdul: I have the Bangladeshi ones, naga, very hot. One time I put two in the fish curry, my partner Shirin, she was crying. Water, water! Now she watches me when I cook.
Gurpreet: Ha! Naga, yes, very strong. I don't touch that one.
Abdul: You cook also?
Gurpreet: Little bit. Aloo parathas on my day off. And in gurdwara, langar, on gurpurab, we cook for big numbers, hundreds people.
Abdul: Hundreds! That's proper cooking. I learned in restaurants, Brick Lane, long time ago. Big pots, big fire. Now I do Sunday dinner for the family, my stepson comes, Rayhan. He eats like three people.
Gurpreet: Young boys, yeah, yeah. Always hungry.
Abdul: Always. What you do for work, Gurpreet?
Gurpreet: Food factory near Heathrow. Tray-sealing. Part-time, because my back.
Abdul: Ah, back. Sorry to hear. I'm a porter, hospital, Whitechapel, I see lots of backs. Lot of porters, we have problem with back, knees. My knees, they're starting now. What happened to yours?
Gurpreet: Lifting, the film rolls. Two years ago. It's okay now, little bit hard sometimes. I walk, Lake Farm, slowly.
Abdul: Walking is the best. Doctors always tell this. Slowly, slowly, but every day.
Gurpreet: Yes. Physio said same. You are walking a lot in the hospital, innit?
Abdul: Twenty thousand steps! I told Hitesh before, the hospital is my gym. He said he bowls fast. I didn't argue with him.
Gurpreet: Ha. I talked to Nilesh before you, he does same job as me. Same machine.
Abdul: Nilesh, yes, nice man, quiet. I spoke to him first. He looks after his dad. Good boy.
Gurpreet: Yeah, he seems very good. My parents are in Punjab. I call my mum every evening, video call.
Abdul: Every evening, that's very good. My father, er, he passed when I was here, so... call your mum. Every evening, keep doing it.
Gurpreet: Yeah. I will. Sorry about your father.
Abdul: Thank you. Long time now. You go back to Punjab sometimes?
Gurpreet: Every two years, in winter. But flights to Amritsar now, so expensive, every year going up.
Abdul: Sylhet same! I look at the price, I close the laptop, I open it again next day, maybe it's cheaper. Never cheaper.
Gurpreet: Never, yeah, yeah. Same with the cash and carry, everything—

=== CALL C0027 ===
Hitesh: Hello! Sat sri akal, ji! Can you hear me?
Gurpreet: Sat sri akal! Yes, I can hear you. Hello. How are you?
Hitesh: Good, good. Last one, yeah? Everybody else is finished, it's just me and you now. Hitesh, Peterborough.
Gurpreet: Gurpreet. Hayes, West London. Nice to meet you.
Hitesh: Hayes, near airport, yeah? I spoke to Marta, she said you were very patient with the puzzle. Better than me.
Gurpreet: Ha, no, no. I was slow, that's it. I don't know I got it right.
Hitesh: Slow is fine, mate. I just clicked anything. What you do for work?
Gurpreet: Food factory, near Heathrow. Tray-sealing line. Part-time, three shifts.
Hitesh: Three shifts! Same as me! Chilled food, Peterborough, I'm on flow-wrap, but I do tray-sealer also sometimes. When the machine jams, they call me, you know, I know all the shortcuts.
Gurpreet: Shortcuts, yeah, yeah. Everybody has shortcuts on the machine.
Hitesh: Some shortcuts the supervisor doesn't like, ha. Why part-time for you? For me it's choice, I do delivery also, moped, evenings.
Gurpreet: Er, my back. Two years ago I hurt it, lifting the film rolls. Physio said do less. It's okay now. Little bit hard sometimes.
Hitesh: Ah, sorry, mate. Those rolls, they're stupid heavy. They should give machine for that. You do forklift also?
Gurpreet: Yes, I have the licence. From work, they paid.
Hitesh: They paid! Lucky. I'm driving forklift sometimes, but no licence, you know, just when nobody is looking. I keep saying I'll book the course. Warehouse pays better, innit.
Gurpreet: Yeah, it's better. It's not so hard, the course. Few days. You should do it.
Hitesh: Yeah, yeah. I should. My wife says same. Every year I say this year. Like Dubai, I say every year. Where you're from, Punjab?
Gurpreet: Yes, near Phagwara, Jalandhar side. I came at twenty-four.
Hitesh: I came twenty-six! Gujarat, Anand district. Married, came here, boom, factory. I was doing BCom, didn't finish, you know. Sometimes I think, if I stayed...
Gurpreet: Yeah. Same for many people. I did ITI, fitting. Here nobody cares, you start again.
Hitesh: Exactly! Here they see you on the line, they think you're just a line guy. They don't know what's in here. But anyway, I have ideas. Phone repair stall, maybe. I can fix any phone.
Gurpreet: Sorry? Phone what?
Hitesh: Phone repair. Screens, unlocking. I worked in my cousin's shop back home, years. You have broken phone, send it to Peterborough, I fix it, special price.
Gurpreet: Ha. Okay, okay. My phone is fine, thank god. You watch cricket?
Hitesh: Watch? Mate, I live cricket. IPL, Mumbai Indians. Last night, our guy, dropped catch, simple. I told uncle Abdul, I told Marta, now I'm telling you. Everyone must know.
Gurpreet: Yeah, I saw it. Very easy one. I watch India mostly, World Cup, big matches. Not every IPL.
Hitesh: Not every IPL? Gurpreet ji, what are you doing with your evenings?
Gurpreet: Er, I call my mum. Every evening, video call. And I look after my chillies.
Hitesh: Chillies! Abdul uncle has chillies also, on the balcony. Every Indian man in this study is growing chillies except me. I just buy them from Lincoln Road. Komal says I should grow something, I said, I'm growing the kids, that's enough.
Gurpreet: Ha! That's also growing, yeah, yeah. How old are your kids?
Hitesh: Dev is twelve, Riya eight. Dev wants new phone for birthday, iPhone. I said, I fix phones, I give you good old one. He said, Papa, no, everyone will—

=== CALL C0028 ===
Hitesh: Hello! Kem cho, bhai? Can you hear me?
Nilesh: Ha, yeah, I can hear you. Erm, majama. That's about as far as my Gujarati goes, to be honest.
Hitesh: Ha! London Gujarati, I know. Hitesh, Peterborough. I said to Gurpreet before, last call, finished, but no, they give me one more. Good, I like talking.
Nilesh: Nilesh. Kingsbury. Nice to meet you. I saw your photo, you've got the Ganesh calendar.
Hitesh: Free one, from the grocery shop! You also have Ganesh, the little shrine. And same hoodie, look, navy. We're twins, mate.
Nilesh: Ha, yeah, we are a bit. Erm, so what do you do?
Hitesh: Chilled food factory, flow-wrap machine. Part-time, but I do delivery also, moped, evenings. With both, I'm making more than full-time guys, easy.
Nilesh: Oh, right. That's good. I'm in chilled food as well, Park Royal. Tray-sealer, full-time, rotating shifts.
Hitesh: Everybody in this study is chilled food! Gurpreet also, tray-sealer. They put all the factory guys together. How long you're there?
Nilesh: Eleven years now. I train the new starters on the sealer, sort of thing. They're talking about team leader, maybe.
Hitesh: Team leader, that's good, take it, mate. More money. Me, they should make me team leader, I know every shortcut, but supervisor doesn't like me. Two warnings, for lateness. Bus is always late, what can I do?
Nilesh: Yeah, the North Circular's the same for me. Nightmare most mornings.
Hitesh: You drive forklift?
Nilesh: Yeah, I've got the counterbalance licence. Work put me through it.
Hitesh: Everybody has licence except me! Gurpreet also. I'm driving it, no licence. Okay, okay, I will book it. Three people told me today.
Nilesh: Honestly, it's only a few days. Worth it.
Hitesh: You watch IPL?
Nilesh: Yeah, with my dad, mostly. He gets really into it. Erm, he's not been so well lately, so it's sort of our thing now, you know, sitting together.
Hitesh: That's nice. That's very nice. My father is in Gujarat, he's also not well. I can't sit with him, I only argue on WhatsApp about cricket. Your dad is close?
Nilesh: Ten minutes, in Kenton. My mum keeps sending dinner round, so I can't complain.
Hitesh: Lucky man. Me, my brother is in Leicester, he has shop, doing very well, he can go to India whenever. I'm, you know, factory. Anyway. Sorry, sorry, what was I saying?
Nilesh: Erm, your dad, but it's fine. Do you get back much?
Hitesh: Every two, three years. Should be more. You go India?
Nilesh: Once, 2019, cousin's wedding. Hot, loud, lovely. My parents came from Kenya, actually, so I'd like to take the kids there one day, see where my dad grew up.
Hitesh: Kenya Gujarati! So that's why your Gujarati is broken, ha. Sorry, sorry, joking.
Nilesh: No, it's true. My mum says the same thing every week.
Hitesh: Your kids speak?
Nilesh: Not really. That's sort of what bothers me, you know. I can't teach them what I haven't got.
Hitesh: Send them to Peterborough for summer, Komal will teach them in one week. My kids, Gujarati at home, all the time. Dev answers in English, cheeky boy, but he—

=== CALL C0029 ===
Marta: Hi! Hello! Can you hear me okay?
Abdul: Yes, yes, perfect. Hello! Abdul. And you're Marta, the lady with the books!
Marta: Ha, everyone's saying that today. Yes, that's me. How are you doing?
Abdul: Good, thank you, little bit tired. Late shift yesterday. How about you, how is your day?
Marta: Erm, long. I'm a pharmacist, cardiology wards, so lots of drug charts. And I'm a bit shattered. Where are you based?
Abdul: Leyton. East London.
Marta: No way! I'm in Walthamstow, just off Hoe Street. And I swim at the Leyton pool, the freezing one.
Abdul: Ah, the leisure centre! I walk past it every day. Neighbours, we are! And hospital also, I'm a porter, Whitechapel. Sixteen years.
Marta: Oh, I love porters, honestly. You lot keep the whole place running. When a porter doesn't come, nothing moves. The patient's stuck, the bed's stuck, the doctors are stuck.
Abdul: Thank you! Nobody says this! Tell my manager, please.
Marta: I will, I'll write a letter. Do you enjoy it?
Abdul: Yes, I like it. I like the patients. Old people especially, they're frightened, so I talk, talk. Some of them, nobody comes to visit. Weeks, nobody. Those ones, I remember them, you know. They stay with you.
Marta: Yeah. Yeah, I know exactly what you mean. I counsel people before discharge, and sometimes there's just no one to explain things to except them, and you worry, will they manage the tablets on their own at home?
Abdul: That's it. You go home, you're still thinking.
Marta: Totally. Sorry, that got serious quickly! Your photo, I saw the chillies on the balcony. My tomatoes are finally going red.
Abdul: Tomatoes, I have also! Few pots. And the chillies, this year very good. Gurpreet has chillies also, we talked a long time. Chilli club.
Marta: Can I join with tomatoes, or is it chillies only?
Abdul: You can join, tomatoes allowed. Do you cook?
Marta: I do most weeknights. Polish things, żurek, gołąbki, and I do a dal, but probably not a very good one.
Abdul: I'm sure it's good. I'm cooking Sunday, fish curry, bhuna. I learned in Brick Lane restaurants long time ago. Shirin does the weekdays.
Marta: Oh, that sounds amazing. Is there anywhere local you'd recommend? We always end up at the same places.
Abdul: The Turkish grill near Leyton Midland Road. Very good. Mixed grill, big plate, you won't eat dinner the next day.
Marta: Okay, I'm telling Daniel tonight. He'll be thrilled, he's been marking all weekend. Do you have a sweet tooth? I bake a lot for work.
Abdul: Sweet, oh yes. But Shirin is making me cut the sugar in my tea. Three spoons, now two. Next year one, she says.
Marta: Two is still very respectable, honestly. As a pharmacist I'm not allowed to say that.
Abdul: Ha! I won't tell anybody. So you're from where, originally?
Marta: Gdańsk, in Poland. Fifteen years here, though, so I'm sort of half and half now. Bit foreign in both places, if that makes sense.
Abdul: It makes sense. Thirty years for me, since 1993. I go to Sylhet, they say, ah, the London man. I come back here, they say—

calls.C0021:
Abdul: Hello, hello! Can you hear me okay?
Nilesh: Yeah, I can hear you fine. Hi.
Abdul: Good, good. I'm Abdul. How are you doing today?
Nilesh: Not bad, thanks. Bit knackered, to be honest. I was on a late last night, so, erm, yeah. You?
Abdul: Late shift? Yeah, me also, yesterday! I'm a porter at the hospital in Whitechapel, and the lifts in the old block broke down again, so I'm pushing the beds round the long way, you know, half the building. My legs are telling me about it today.
Nilesh: Oh no. That sounds rough.
Abdul: It's okay, it's the job, innit. Sixteen years I'm doing it. What about you, what you do?
Nilesh: Erm, I work in a factory, chilled food, in Park Royal. I run a tray-sealing machine on the packing line. Ready meals, that sort of thing.
Abdul: Ah, so the ones in the supermarket, the little trays with the film on top?
Nilesh: Yeah, that's us. Well, some of them. I've been there eleven years now, so I sort of... I train the new starters on the sealer as well, when they come in.
Abdul: Eleven years, that's good, that's loyal. Same as me, they give me the new porters to show around, because I know every corridor. You must be patient, yeah? To train people.
Nilesh: I try to be. Erm, when I started someone was a bit sharp with me, and I remember how that felt, so I just take it slow with them, you know. Nobody learns anything if they're scared of the machine.
Abdul: Exactly, exactly. Same with patients. Old lady, she's frightened going down to the scan, I just keep talking, talking, about the weather, cricket, anything. By the time we get there she's forgot she was worried.
Nilesh: That's nice, actually. I reckon the nurses must like you.
Abdul: They ask for me by name sometimes! Makes me feel very important. Do you follow cricket at all?
Nilesh: Yeah, more than football really. I listen to the Tests on the radio app on my break. Though England... another collapse, wasn't it.
Abdul: Don't talk to me about collapse! Bangladesh, last week, I was sure, sure they're going to win. I told my friends, I said relax, this one is easy. Then three wickets in two overs. Finished.
Nilesh: Oh, I saw that. That was painful.
Abdul: Painful, yes. I used to play, Sunday tape-ball in Victoria Park, but my knees, after forty-five, they said no more, Abdul. Now I just umpire. Shout at everybody instead.
Nilesh: Ha. I play five-a-side with my cousins every couple of weeks, but they stick me in goal, so I don't have to run much.
Abdul: Smart man! Goalkeeper is the best job. And the puzzle at the start, how did you find it? I was stuck on the third one a long time.
Nilesh: Erm, the one with the shapes? Yeah, I didn't finish it, to be honest. I sort of guessed the last two.
Abdul: Me too, guessing! I put my glasses on, I thought they would help, but no.
Nilesh: Ha, yeah. Do you get many days off, with the rota?
Abdul: Not so many. I am saving my leave, I go back to Sylhet every two, three years, so I take one month together. You have family round you?
Nilesh: Yeah, my parents are in Kenton, ten minutes away. My mum keeps sending food round, which, erm, I'm not complaining about. My dad's... he's slowing down a bit lately, so it's good being close, you know.
Abdul: That's a blessing, being close. Really. Look after him. You only get them once.
Nilesh: Yeah. I try.
Abdul: You're a good son, I can tell. So do you cover shifts, at your place, when they ask?
Nilesh: Erm, more than I should, probably. I find it hard to say no, sort of, and then I'm—
calls.C0022:
Marta: Hi! Hello, can you hear me? Sorry, I think I was on mute for a second.
Gurpreet: Yes, yes, I can hear you. Hello. How are you?
Marta: I'm good, thank you, a bit shattered, but good. I'm Marta. And you're Gurpreet?
Gurpreet: Yeah, Gurpreet. Nice to meet you. You had busy day?
Marta: Erm, sort of, yeah. I'm a pharmacist at a hospital, on the cardiology wards, so it's lots of checking drug charts and talking to patients before they go home, you know, explaining their blood thinners and things. And the Victoria line this morning was absolutely rammed, I had someone's elbow in my face the whole way. What about you, what do you do?
Gurpreet: Er, I work in factory near Heathrow. Food packaging. I run the tray-sealing line, for ready meals, sandwiches, like that.
Marta: Oh, so the sandwiches people buy at the airport?
Gurpreet: Yeah, yeah, some of them going to airport, some supermarket. I'm part-time now, three shifts in a week.
Marta: That sounds quite nice, actually, part-time. Is that your choice?
Gurpreet: Er, yeah, sort of. I hurt my back two years ago, so the physio said little bit less. It's okay now. Little bit hard sometimes, but okay.
Marta: Oh, I'm sorry. Backs are horrible, honestly. We see so many people on the ward who've been, you know, lifting things for thirty years. Do you do exercises for it?
Gurpreet: I walk. Lake Farm, near my place, in Hayes. I do slow lap, every day off. That's it, really.
Marta: That's lovely. I swim, or I try to, twice a week before work, but the pool in Leyton is always freezing, so sometimes I kind of stand at the edge and think about it and then go home.
Gurpreet: Ha. Cold water, no, I can't.
Marta: And what do you do on the weekends, apart from walking?
Gurpreet: Sunday I go gurdwara in Southall, mostly. And I'm growing chillies and coriander in pots, on the patio. This year chillies are doing really well, I don't know why.
Marta: No way! I'm growing tomatoes in our tiny garden and they've finally, finally gone red. I was so excited I sent a photo to my mum in Poland.
Gurpreet: Ah, you're from Poland? Nice.
Marta: Yeah, from Gdańsk, but I've been here fifteen years now, so I'm kind of half and half. What chillies are they?
Gurpreet: Er, green ones, the small hot ones, like we use in India. My partner Simran says too many now, we have to give to neighbours.
Marta: That's the best problem to have. Is Simran into the gardening too?
Gurpreet: Not so much. She's teaching assistant, primary school, so she's tired after work, the kids, you know. She likes eating the chillies, not growing.
Marta: Ha, yeah, no, totally. My husband's the same with my tomatoes, he just appears when they're ready. He's a teacher as well, actually, geography. He spends the whole weekend marking at the kitchen table, and our cat sits on the paper.
Gurpreet: You have cat?
Marta: We do, Pierogi. He's a tabby and he's, erm, a bit round. He knocks everything off the worktop, one thing a day, like it's his job.
Gurpreet: Pierogi, like the food?
Marta: Exactly like the food! Polish dumplings. He looks like one, honestly. Sorry, I'm talking so much. How did you find the puzzle at the start?
Gurpreet: Er, it was okay. Last one was hard, I took long time. I think maybe I got it.
Marta: Better than me, I gave up on the last one and just stared at it.
Gurpreet: That's okay, no problem. Everybody is like that, innit, with puzzles. Like my cousin, he—
calls.C0023:
Hitesh: Hello! Yeah, there he is. Can you hear me, uncle? Sorry, sorry, can I call you uncle? Your photo, you look like proper uncle.
Abdul: Ha! Yes, yes, call me what you like. Abdul. Everybody at work calls me uncle anyway, even the doctors.
Hitesh: Hitesh. Peterborough. Where you are?
Abdul: Leyton, East London. Thirty years I'm in East London. You're in Peterborough, very nice. What you do there?
Hitesh: Factory, chilled food, I'm on flow-wrap machine. Basically I'm the guy who knows how to fix it when it jams, you know, supervisor comes to me. Part-time, but that's my choice, yeah, because I do delivery also, and my own business ideas, so.
Abdul: Business ideas! Good, good. What kind of business?
Hitesh: Er, phones, maybe. I used to work in my cousin's phone shop back home, Gujarat, I can unlock anything, fix screen, anything. Or taxi licence. Or, you know, investments.
Abdul: Investments, ah. Shares and all that?
Hitesh: Bit of crypto, bit of shares. Some up, some down, that's the game, innit. You have to be in it.
Abdul: Me, I don't understand it. My money goes in the bank and then to my sister's kids for school. That's my investment.
Hitesh: That's also good, mate. Safe. What's your job?
Abdul: Hospital porter, Whitechapel. Sixteen years. Pushing beds, wheelchairs, oxygen, everything. Twenty thousand steps a shift, my shoes finished every few months.
Hitesh: Twenty thousand! You don't need gym then.
Abdul: No gym. The hospital is my gym. You play any sport?
Hitesh: Cricket, mate. Sunday, tape-ball, in the park, with the guys. Mostly for the banter, but I'm good, I bowl fast. And IPL, every match. Mumbai Indians.
Abdul: Mumbai! Ah. I play tape-ball also, Victoria Park, until my knees said no. Now I umpire. And I'm Bangladesh, of course.
Hitesh: Bangladesh, oh no. Sorry, uncle. Last week, that match...
Abdul: Don't. I was talking about this one already today with the gentleman before, Nilesh. Three wickets in two overs. I am still not sleeping properly.
Hitesh: Ha! At least they lost properly. Mumbai, last night, our guy drops simple catch. Simple! My son Dev could catch that, and he's twelve. I was shouting at the TV, my wife says the neighbours will complain.
Abdul: The umpire in me says it's a hard catch maybe. The fan in me says, no, he should catch.
Hitesh: No, no, uncle, no hard catch. Straight in the hands. I was saying to my brother on WhatsApp, this guy should be dropped himself. Big argument in the family group now.
Abdul: Family group, yes, we have one too, everybody in Sylhet, everybody in London, all shouting. You have big family here?
Hitesh: Brother in Leicester. He has shop there. Doing well, you know, he's... yeah, he's doing well. Parents are in India still. My father, er, his health is not so great now.
Abdul: Ah. I'm sorry to hear. You go back often?
Hitesh: Every two, three years, for the weddings mostly. Should be more. But tickets, holidays, work, you know how it is.
Abdul: I know. I know exactly. Me also, I save one month leave, then go. It's never enough. Call him a lot, that's what I say. Phone is free now.
Hitesh: Yeah. Yeah, I do. My wife says I talk more to the cricket than to my dad, but... anyway. Sorry, sorry, what was the question? I'm going everywhere.
Abdul: No question! We are just chatting, it's fine. Tell me, the puzzle at the start, you finished it?
Hitesh: Puzzle, honestly, mate, waste of time. I did the first two fast, then the last one, I thought, who is checking? I just clicked something.
Abdul: Ha! Same as Nilesh, he's guessing also. I think nobody finished, only the researchers.
Hitesh: They make it, so they know the answer, innit. Easy for them. Like my supervisor, he makes the rules, then he—
calls.C0024:
Nilesh: Hi. Hello. Can you hear me alright?
Gurpreet: Yes, I can hear you. Hello. How are you?
Nilesh: Yeah, not bad, thanks. Bit tired. You?
Gurpreet: I'm okay, thank you. Little bit tired also. I'm Gurpreet.
Nilesh: Nilesh. Nice to meet you.
Gurpreet: Nice to meet you. Where you are, which area?
Nilesh: Kingsbury, North West London. You?
Gurpreet: Hayes. West side, near Heathrow.
Nilesh: Oh right, not too far then. What do you do?
Gurpreet: I work in food factory, packaging, near the airport. I run the tray-sealing line.
Nilesh: No way. Tray-sealing? That's what I do. Park Royal, chilled food. Ready meals mostly.
Gurpreet: Really? Same machine! Ready meals, sandwiches, yeah, yeah.
Nilesh: That's funny. The man I spoke to before, Abdul, he asked me about the little trays with the film on top, and I was trying to explain, and now here's someone who actually knows.
Gurpreet: Ha. Nobody knows what we do, really. They just buy the lasagne.
Nilesh: Exactly. Erm, how long have you been doing it?
Gurpreet: Er, long time, maybe ten years, different places. Now I'm part-time, three shifts, because my back. I hurt it two years ago, so the physio said, you know, little bit less.
Nilesh: Oh, sorry to hear that. Was it at work?
Gurpreet: Yeah, sort of. Lifting the film rolls, I think, too many times wrong way. It's okay now. Little bit hard sometimes.
Nilesh: Yeah, those rolls are heavy. We had a lad do the same last year. I always tell the new starters, get the trolley, don't be a hero, you know.
Gurpreet: Yeah, yeah, good advice. You train the new people?
Nilesh: Yeah, on the sealer, mostly. They keep asking me. I don't mind, really. They're thinking about team leader for me, maybe, but erm, I'm not sure. Half the line are my mates, so telling them off would be, sort of, weird.
Gurpreet: I did team leader cover one time. Two weeks. Very hard. One guy always late, I have to talk to him, I don't like it. I'm happy to go back to machine.
Nilesh: Yeah, that's exactly what worries me. The money would be nice, though. We're trying to save for a deposit, so.
Gurpreet: Same, me and Simran, my partner. We are saving. London is very expensive, so maybe Slough, something small.
Nilesh: Yeah. It feels like it's always just out of reach, you know.
Gurpreet: Yeah. Slowly, slowly. That's it, really.
Nilesh: Do they change your overtime rota a lot? Ours changes every week.
Gurpreet: Every week! I look on Monday, it's one thing, Wednesday, something else. And people ask me to swap, I always say yes.
Nilesh: Ha, me too. I can't say no. My wife says I should, but then I'm stood there and they look at you, and—
calls.C0025:
Hitesh: Hello! Yes, I can see you. The happy lady with the books!
Marta: Ha! That's me, yeah. Hi, I'm Marta. Sorry, the books are a bit of a mess, I keep meaning to sort them out.
Hitesh: No, no, it looks good. My daughter Riya, she's eight, she wants a shelf like that. Hitesh, Peterborough. Where you're from? I hear little bit accent.
Marta: Yeah, Poland, Gdańsk, but I've lived in London fifteen years now. Walthamstow. What about you?
Hitesh: Gujarat, India. Came 2008, I married, wife's family was in Peterborough, so, Peterborough. What's your job?
Marta: I'm a pharmacist, in a hospital, on the heart wards. Erm, so I check everyone's medication and talk to patients before they go home.
Hitesh: Pharmacist! My wife, Komal, she works in pharmacy also. Counter, in the shop. She knows all the tablets, she tells me what to take, I don't listen.
Marta: Ha, that's what all my patients say about their wives. Does she enjoy it?
Hitesh: Yeah, she likes it. Full-time. She's the organised one, you know, bills, school forms, holidays, everything. Me, I'm the fun one.
Marta: Every house needs both, honestly. I'm the organised one in ours. I plan our holidays on spreadsheets, my husband just turns up at the airport.
Hitesh: Spreadsheet for holiday! No, mate. Too much. You just go.
Marta: I know, I know, but I like it, it's kind of half the fun for me. Where do you like to go?
Hitesh: India, mostly, weddings. Blackpool with the kids, London. And Dubai, my friend works there, I'm going this year. Definitely. Well, I say every year.
Marta: Oh, you should, though. Who books it, you or Komal?
Hitesh: Komal, obviously. Then I complain about flight time. Six in the morning, why, who flies six in the morning?
Marta: People who get the cheap flights! Sorry, that sounded like a spreadsheet person.
Hitesh: Ha! Yes, very spreadsheet. What you do, then, I'm in factory, flow-wrap machine, part-time. I do delivery also, moped, evenings. Good money, you know, if you know the right areas.
Marta: Oh, so you're working quite a lot of hours then, with both?
Hitesh: Er, depends. Part-time is my choice. Rules at the factory, mate, half of them pointless. Supervisor wants you standing there even when the machine is running perfectly.
Marta: I mean, we have loads of rules on the ward too, and some of them do feel a bit silly, but, erm, usually there's a story behind each one. Someone got hurt once, you know.
Hitesh: Maybe. Maybe. But some of them, no story, just somebody in an office. Anyway. Did you do the puzzle?
Marta: Badly. I gave up on the last one. Gurpreet, who I spoke to first, was much more patient than me.
Hitesh: Gurpreet, he looks like he knows his stuff. I just clicked anything. Uncle Abdul, he also, guessing. Nobody finished, I think.
Marta: That makes me feel better, honestly. So what do you do to relax, when you're not working?
Hitesh: Cricket. Watching, playing, Sunday in the park. And last night, Mumbai Indians, our guy drops simple catch, I'm still angry.
Marta: I don't really know cricket, to be honest, but my husband's English, so I've been made to watch some. It goes on for days, right?
Hitesh: Test, yes, five days, that's for old men. IPL is three hours, fast, everybody hitting sixes. Much better. You watch one with me, I explain, you'll love it.
Marta: Okay, deal, but you have to sit through a whole Polish volleyball match with—
calls.C0026:
Abdul: Hello, hello! Gurpreet, yes?
Gurpreet: Yes, hello. How are you?
Abdul: Good, good, thank you. Abdul, from Leyton. And how are you, my friend?
Gurpreet: I'm okay, thank you. I saw your photo, you have chillies on balcony, yeah?
Abdul: Yes! You saw them! Nobody notices my chillies. Yes, few pots. This year better than last year.
Gurpreet: Me also. I grow chillies and coriander, on the patio, Hayes. This year very good, too many. Simran says give to neighbours.
Abdul: Same, same! What kind you grow?
Gurpreet: Green ones, small, the hot ones. From India seeds, my cousin brought.
Abdul: I have the Bangladeshi ones, naga, very hot. One time I put two in the fish curry, my partner Shirin, she was crying. Water, water! Now she watches me when I cook.
Gurpreet: Ha! Naga, yes, very strong. I don't touch that one.
Abdul: You cook also?
Gurpreet: Little bit. Aloo parathas on my day off. And in gurdwara, langar, on gurpurab, we cook for big numbers, hundreds people.
Abdul: Hundreds! That's proper cooking. I learned in restaurants, Brick Lane, long time ago. Big pots, big fire. Now I do Sunday dinner for the family, my stepson comes, Rayhan. He eats like three people.
Gurpreet: Young boys, yeah, yeah. Always hungry.
Abdul: Always. What you do for work, Gurpreet?
Gurpreet: Food factory near Heathrow. Tray-sealing. Part-time, because my back.
Abdul: Ah, back. Sorry to hear. I'm a porter, hospital, Whitechapel, I see lots of backs. Lot of porters, we have problem with back, knees. My knees, they're starting now. What happened to yours?
Gurpreet: Lifting, the film rolls. Two years ago. It's okay now, little bit hard sometimes. I walk, Lake Farm, slowly.
Abdul: Walking is the best. Doctors always tell this. Slowly, slowly, but every day.
Gurpreet: Yes. Physio said same. You are walking a lot in the hospital, innit?
Abdul: Twenty thousand steps! I told Hitesh before, the hospital is my gym. He said he bowls fast. I didn't argue with him.
Gurpreet: Ha. I talked to Nilesh before you, he does same job as me. Same machine.
Abdul: Nilesh, yes, nice man, quiet. I spoke to him first. He looks after his dad. Good boy.
Gurpreet: Yeah, he seems very good. My parents are in Punjab. I call my mum every evening, video call.
Abdul: Every evening, that's very good. My father, er, he passed when I was here, so... call your mum. Every evening, keep doing it.
Gurpreet: Yeah. I will. Sorry about your father.
Abdul: Thank you. Long time now. You go back to Punjab sometimes?
Gurpreet: Every two years, in winter. But flights to Amritsar now, so expensive, every year going up.
Abdul: Sylhet same! I look at the price, I close the laptop, I open it again next day, maybe it's cheaper. Never cheaper.
Gurpreet: Never, yeah, yeah. Same with the cash and carry, everything—
calls.C0027:
Hitesh: Hello! Sat sri akal, ji! Can you hear me?
Gurpreet: Sat sri akal! Yes, I can hear you. Hello. How are you?
Hitesh: Good, good. Last one, yeah? Everybody else is finished, it's just me and you now. Hitesh, Peterborough.
Gurpreet: Gurpreet. Hayes, West London. Nice to meet you.
Hitesh: Hayes, near airport, yeah? I spoke to Marta, she said you were very patient with the puzzle. Better than me.
Gurpreet: Ha, no, no. I was slow, that's it. I don't know I got it right.
Hitesh: Slow is fine, mate. I just clicked anything. What you do for work?
Gurpreet: Food factory, near Heathrow. Tray-sealing line. Part-time, three shifts.
Hitesh: Three shifts! Same as me! Chilled food, Peterborough, I'm on flow-wrap, but I do tray-sealer also sometimes. When the machine jams, they call me, you know, I know all the shortcuts.
Gurpreet: Shortcuts, yeah, yeah. Everybody has shortcuts on the machine.
Hitesh: Some shortcuts the supervisor doesn't like, ha. Why part-time for you? For me it's choice, I do delivery also, moped, evenings.
Gurpreet: Er, my back. Two years ago I hurt it, lifting the film rolls. Physio said do less. It's okay now. Little bit hard sometimes.
Hitesh: Ah, sorry, mate. Those rolls, they're stupid heavy. They should give machine for that. You do forklift also?
Gurpreet: Yes, I have the licence. From work, they paid.
Hitesh: They paid! Lucky. I'm driving forklift sometimes, but no licence, you know, just when nobody is looking. I keep saying I'll book the course. Warehouse pays better, innit.
Gurpreet: Yeah, it's better. It's not so hard, the course. Few days. You should do it.
Hitesh: Yeah, yeah. I should. My wife says same. Every year I say this year. Like Dubai, I say every year. Where you're from, Punjab?
Gurpreet: Yes, near Phagwara, Jalandhar side. I came at twenty-four.
Hitesh: I came twenty-six! Gujarat, Anand district. Married, came here, boom, factory. I was doing BCom, didn't finish, you know. Sometimes I think, if I stayed...
Gurpreet: Yeah. Same for many people. I did ITI, fitting. Here nobody cares, you start again.
Hitesh: Exactly! Here they see you on the line, they think you're just a line guy. They don't know what's in here. But anyway, I have ideas. Phone repair stall, maybe. I can fix any phone.
Gurpreet: Sorry? Phone what?
Hitesh: Phone repair. Screens, unlocking. I worked in my cousin's shop back home, years. You have broken phone, send it to Peterborough, I fix it, special price.
Gurpreet: Ha. Okay, okay. My phone is fine, thank god. You watch cricket?
Hitesh: Watch? Mate, I live cricket. IPL, Mumbai Indians. Last night, our guy, dropped catch, simple. I told uncle Abdul, I told Marta, now I'm telling you. Everyone must know.
Gurpreet: Yeah, I saw it. Very easy one. I watch India mostly, World Cup, big matches. Not every IPL.
Hitesh: Not every IPL? Gurpreet ji, what are you doing with your evenings?
Gurpreet: Er, I call my mum. Every evening, video call. And I look after my chillies.
Hitesh: Chillies! Abdul uncle has chillies also, on the balcony. Every Indian man in this study is growing chillies except me. I just buy them from Lincoln Road. Komal says I should grow something, I said, I'm growing the kids, that's enough.
Gurpreet: Ha! That's also growing, yeah, yeah. How old are your kids?
Hitesh: Dev is twelve, Riya eight. Dev wants new phone for birthday, iPhone. I said, I fix phones, I give you good old one. He said, Papa, no, everyone will—
calls.C0028:
Hitesh: Hello! Kem cho, bhai? Can you hear me?
Nilesh: Ha, yeah, I can hear you. Erm, majama. That's about as far as my Gujarati goes, to be honest.
Hitesh: Ha! London Gujarati, I know. Hitesh, Peterborough. I said to Gurpreet before, last call, finished, but no, they give me one more. Good, I like talking.
Nilesh: Nilesh. Kingsbury. Nice to meet you. I saw your photo, you've got the Ganesh calendar.
Hitesh: Free one, from the grocery shop! You also have Ganesh, the little shrine. And same hoodie, look, navy. We're twins, mate.
Nilesh: Ha, yeah, we are a bit. Erm, so what do you do?
Hitesh: Chilled food factory, flow-wrap machine. Part-time, but I do delivery also, moped, evenings. With both, I'm making more than full-time guys, easy.
Nilesh: Oh, right. That's good. I'm in chilled food as well, Park Royal. Tray-sealer, full-time, rotating shifts.
Hitesh: Everybody in this study is chilled food! Gurpreet also, tray-sealer. They put all the factory guys together. How long you're there?
Nilesh: Eleven years now. I train the new starters on the sealer, sort of thing. They're talking about team leader, maybe.
Hitesh: Team leader, that's good, take it, mate. More money. Me, they should make me team leader, I know every shortcut, but supervisor doesn't like me. Two warnings, for lateness. Bus is always late, what can I do?
Nilesh: Yeah, the North Circular's the same for me. Nightmare most mornings.
Hitesh: You drive forklift?
Nilesh: Yeah, I've got the counterbalance licence. Work put me through it.
Hitesh: Everybody has licence except me! Gurpreet also. I'm driving it, no licence. Okay, okay, I will book it. Three people told me today.
Nilesh: Honestly, it's only a few days. Worth it.
Hitesh: You watch IPL?
Nilesh: Yeah, with my dad, mostly. He gets really into it. Erm, he's not been so well lately, so it's sort of our thing now, you know, sitting together.
Hitesh: That's nice. That's very nice. My father is in Gujarat, he's also not well. I can't sit with him, I only argue on WhatsApp about cricket. Your dad is close?
Nilesh: Ten minutes, in Kenton. My mum keeps sending dinner round, so I can't complain.
Hitesh: Lucky man. Me, my brother is in Leicester, he has shop, doing very well, he can go to India whenever. I'm, you know, factory. Anyway. Sorry, sorry, what was I saying?
Nilesh: Erm, your dad, but it's fine. Do you get back much?
Hitesh: Every two, three years. Should be more. You go India?
Nilesh: Once, 2019, cousin's wedding. Hot, loud, lovely. My parents came from Kenya, actually, so I'd like to take the kids there one day, see where my dad grew up.
Hitesh: Kenya Gujarati! So that's why your Gujarati is broken, ha. Sorry, sorry, joking.
Nilesh: No, it's true. My mum says the same thing every week.
Hitesh: Your kids speak?
Nilesh: Not really. That's sort of what bothers me, you know. I can't teach them what I haven't got.
Hitesh: Send them to Peterborough for summer, Komal will teach them in one week. My kids, Gujarati at home, all the time. Dev answers in English, cheeky boy, but he—
calls.C0029:
Marta: Hi! Hello! Can you hear me okay?
Abdul: Yes, yes, perfect. Hello! Abdul. And you're Marta, the lady with the books!
Marta: Ha, everyone's saying that today. Yes, that's me. How are you doing?
Abdul: Good, thank you, little bit tired. Late shift yesterday. How about you, how is your day?
Marta: Erm, long. I'm a pharmacist, cardiology wards, so lots of drug charts. And I'm a bit shattered. Where are you based?
Abdul: Leyton. East London.
Marta: No way! I'm in Walthamstow, just off Hoe Street. And I swim at the Leyton pool, the freezing one.
Abdul: Ah, the leisure centre! I walk past it every day. Neighbours, we are! And hospital also, I'm a porter, Whitechapel. Sixteen years.
Marta: Oh, I love porters, honestly. You lot keep the whole place running. When a porter doesn't come, nothing moves. The patient's stuck, the bed's stuck, the doctors are stuck.
Abdul: Thank you! Nobody says this! Tell my manager, please.
Marta: I will, I'll write a letter. Do you enjoy it?
Abdul: Yes, I like it. I like the patients. Old people especially, they're frightened, so I talk, talk. Some of them, nobody comes to visit. Weeks, nobody. Those ones, I remember them, you know. They stay with you.
Marta: Yeah. Yeah, I know exactly what you mean. I counsel people before discharge, and sometimes there's just no one to explain things to except them, and you worry, will they manage the tablets on their own at home?
Abdul: That's it. You go home, you're still thinking.
Marta: Totally. Sorry, that got serious quickly! Your photo, I saw the chillies on the balcony. My tomatoes are finally going red.
Abdul: Tomatoes, I have also! Few pots. And the chillies, this year very good. Gurpreet has chillies also, we talked a long time. Chilli club.
Marta: Can I join with tomatoes, or is it chillies only?
Abdul: You can join, tomatoes allowed. Do you cook?
Marta: I do most weeknights. Polish things, żurek, gołąbki, and I do a dal, but probably not a very good one.
Abdul: I'm sure it's good. I'm cooking Sunday, fish curry, bhuna. I learned in Brick Lane restaurants long time ago. Shirin does the weekdays.
Marta: Oh, that sounds amazing. Is there anywhere local you'd recommend? We always end up at the same places.
Abdul: The Turkish grill near Leyton Midland Road. Very good. Mixed grill, big plate, you won't eat dinner the next day.
Marta: Okay, I'm telling Daniel tonight. He'll be thrilled, he's been marking all weekend. Do you have a sweet tooth? I bake a lot for work.
Abdul: Sweet, oh yes. But Shirin is making me cut the sugar in my tea. Three spoons, now two. Next year one, she says.
Marta: Two is still very respectable, honestly. As a pharmacist I'm not allowed to say that.
Abdul: Ha! I won't tell anybody. So you're from where, originally?
Marta: Gdańsk, in Poland. Fifteen years here, though, so I'm sort of half and half now. Bit foreign in both places, if that makes sense.
Abdul: It makes sense. Thirty years for me, since 1993. I go to Sylhet, they say, ah, the London man. I come back here, they say—

C0021.line_text: That's a blessing, being close. Really. Look after him. You only get them once.
C0021.what: Before speaking, Abdul goes quiet for about three seconds and looks down and away from the screen. His broad smile drops, he presses his lips together, then looks back up at the camera and speaks more softly than before.
